per_quote.text: The goal of the present research was to examine how political climate moderates the relationship between self-reported political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake. We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023. Controlling for age, education, income, and race, there was an interaction between political conservatism and conservative political climate for both vaccine and booster hesitancy (β = .07, p = .03; β = .12, p < .001, respectively), such that liberals were less likely to be hesitant regardless of political climate. However, conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions. A similar interaction was for the likelihood of receiving a COVID-19 booster (OR =.84, p = .049). Liberals were more likely to receive a booster regardless of political climate, while conservatives’ likelihood was associated with their political climate. Observed patterns linking liberal political climates with vaccine uptake among conservative individuals have important implications for vaccination efforts among conservative individuals in the United States.[page 1]

In the realm of adolescent social network research, the correlation between substance use and friendship formation is well-documented. Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results [47]. Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

Models assessed endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) and actor-level characteristics, including demographic factors, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity.

We employed Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to model the probability of friendship tie formation within each school, accounting for the inherent interdependence of network observations [9,24].

For these cases, we utilized available peer perception data to infer behavior. Participants were asked to nominate up to 10 closest friends and then answer questions about each nominated peer’s behavior...
Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship.

Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample. Sender and receiver effects—indicating whether individuals who use substances are more likely to receive or initiate friendships—were almost entirely non-significant across all three schools and substances.

Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation. These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

Homophily effects provided further evidence of distinct relational logics. Gender and grade homophily were consistently significant across all schools (AME = 0.008–0.058, all p < 0.001), indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.

This finding not only underscores a fundamental lack of theoretical understanding regarding developmental relationship patterns within this demographic but also signals the urgent need to explore more deeply the factors influencing relational dynamics among AI youth.

The findings of this study are not without their limitations. First, we recognize that the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation. The history, policies, geography, and culture of this reservation all intersect with network formation and maintenance patterns.

The cross-sectional design imposes a fundamental interpretive limit: a single, simultaneous observation of the network and of individual attributes cannot capture changes in network formation and behavior over time. More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time.
Third, kinship networks and familial relationships—which operate largely outside the school-based friendship system we measured—may be the primary arena where AI identity shapes social ties.
